897.title: the flute
897.howItsDone: Hindu art and temple images show Krishna holding a flute, and devotees sing songs about it at home and in temples; the Bhagavata's chapter on the flute is read aloud and sung in devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Govardhan lifted: the storm came down on the village, and a boy held up a hill so everyone could shelter underneath. Did you make a little room for someone caught in a storm? Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

A calf is drinking from its mother, and it stops. The milk is still in its mouth. It doesn't swallow. It just stands there with its ears up. Somewhere past the pasture, among the trees, someone is playing a flute. That calf comes from the Bhagavata Purana, from a chapter where the women of Vraja, the gopis, stay behind in the village while Krishna takes the cows out to the forest. They can't see him. They can only hear him. So they start telling each other what the sound is doing to everything it reaches. Today, the flute.
screen: `A CALF FORGETS TO SWALLOW.` → `A FLUTE IN THE TREES.` → `THE GOPIS CAN ONLY HEAR.`

segments.voice: In this chapter Krishna doesn't explain anything or teach anyone. He just plays, walking into the autumn forest with his brother Balarama and the herd. The gopis fill in the picture from memory: a peacock feather in his hair, flowers tucked at his ears, a yellow cloth, a garland of forest flowers, his lips on the bamboo. Then they turn to the listeners, and that list is the heart of the chapter. The cows lift their ears and drink in the sound, and the calves stand with milk in their mouths. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes, listening. The does of the forest gaze at him with their mates beside them. The rivers, the gopis say, slow their current, and reach out with their waves to hold his feet and offer him lotuses. Even the clouds, seeing him walk in the heat, drift over him to give him shade. Look at who is in the audience. Not priests. Not kings. Cows, birds, deer, water, weather. The music goes out to whatever can hear it, and whatever hears it stops what it was doing. Now look at where the gopis are. Not in the forest. At home, at their work, talking. The sound reaches them and he doesn't, and their delight and their ache come from the same place. Some devotional readers hear in this chapter the whole world turned into a listener, every creature called at once. Others simply hear a village falling in love with a sound. Either way, the chapter never stops to explain the flute. It just keeps showing what it does, down to a calf that forgets to swallow.
screen: `HE WALKS INTO THE AUTUMN FOREST.` · `COWS, BIRDS, DEER, RIVERS, CLOUDS.` · `THE GOPIS HEAR, BUT CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `WHAT MAKES A CALF FORGET TO SWALLOW?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your eyes close or soften. For these two minutes, be one of the listeners in the forest. Let sounds come to you without going out to get them: the room, the street, your own breath. Don't name them. Just receive them, the way the cows lift their ears. If a sound pulls you into thinking, come back with the next one. If you pray, you can let one sound stand for the flute, and listen to it as a call. The bell holds the time.
The flute. Krishna's bamboo flute, whose music, the gopis say, stops cows, birds, deer, rivers and clouds in the forest of Vraja.
Your line: the whole forest listening. Today, when a sound catches you, a bird, a song, a voice down the hall, stop for one breath before you move on. Day eight hundred ninety-seven.

898.title: the flute
898.carry: jealous of a reed, then glad
898.howItsDone: Devotees sing and recite the gopis' words about the flute from the Bhagavata, and Krishna is honored under names that mean the one who holds the flute.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flute: the calves stood with milk in their mouths, the birds closed their eyes, and the rivers slowed. Did any sound stop you yesterday? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

What did a stick do to deserve this? That's the gopis' question, and they're not joking. They're still in the village, still listening, and one of them says what the others have been thinking. Krishna's lips are on that flute all day long. It's a length of bamboo, cut from some riverbank. It has no voice of its own, no family, no story. And yet it gets to be closer to him than any of them. So they ask, half in envy and half in wonder: what good thing did this flute ever do? Today the flute again, from the side of the flute.
screen: `WHAT DID A STICK DO?` → `CLOSER TO HIM THAN ANY OF THEM.` → `FROM THE SIDE OF THE FLUTE.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the question to one of the gopis. What virtue, she asks, did this flute practice, that it gets to enjoy the sweetness of his lips, a sweetness the gopis feel belongs to them, and leaves them only what's left over? Then she answers herself in a strange and lovely way. She looks at the bamboo's family. The lakes and rivers whose water raised the bamboo are glad: their lotuses open as if the hair on their skin were standing up. And the trees, the bamboo's elders, let their sap run down like tears, the way old people weep with joy when someone in the family turns out devoted. So the gopi's envy turns, halfway through her sentence, into a kind of praise. Somebody belonging to the riverbank got close to Krishna, and the whole riverbank is proud. Now look at what a flute actually is. A hollow reed. Breath goes in one end and comes out as music, and the flute adds nothing of its own except the empty space. That's the detail some devotional teachers return to: the flute is close to Krishna because there's nothing inside it in the way. They read the gopi's question as the devotee's question, what would it take for me to be that close, and the flute as the answer, a life with room in it. That's an interpretation, not a line in the chapter. The chapter itself just leaves us with a woman in a village, jealous of a piece of bamboo, and then glad for it.
screen: `WHAT GOOD DID THIS FLUTE EVER DO?` · `THE RIVERS AND TREES ARE PROUD.` · `A HOLLOW REED, EMPTY INSIDE.` · then, large: `A LIFE WITH ROOM IN IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. For these two minutes, let your breath be the only thing moving through you, the way breath moves through a reed. Breathe in without grabbing. Breathe out without pushing. Each time you exhale, let one small thing go with it: a plan, a worry, a sentence you were rehearsing. You don't have to empty everything. Just make a little room. If you pray, you can offer the room you've made to Krishna, or to God by any name you use. The bell holds the time.
The flute. A hollow length of bamboo that the gopis envy, because it is always at Krishna's lips.
Your line: jealous of a reed, then glad. Today, when you notice envy for someone, try the gopi's turn: look for one thing in their good luck you can be glad about. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

899.title: the flute
899.tomorrow: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
899.howItsDone: The opening of the rasa lila chapters, with the gopis leaving their work at the sound of the flute, is recited and sung by Krishna devotees, and it is retold in dance and devotional poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flute again: a gopi jealous of a piece of bamboo, until she looked at the rivers and trees that raised it and found herself glad. Did you find one thing to be glad about in someone else's good luck? Day eight hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `JEALOUS OF A REED, THEN GLAD.`

segments.voice: The milk is on the fire. Someone is halfway through milking a cow. Someone is spooning food onto a plate for her family. Someone has a baby at her breast. It's an autumn night in Vraja, the moon is full and coming up red over the trees, and every house is in the middle of something. Then, from the forest, the flute. Not the daytime music the gopis talked about from a distance. This time, the Bhagavata says, the sound is calling them. Today, the flute, and what happens to everything they were holding.
screen: `THE MILK IS ON THE FIRE.` → `A FULL MOON OVER THE TREES.` → `THIS TIME, THE FLUTE CALLS.`

segments.voice: The text slows down here and goes house by house. The women hear the flute and they go, each one exactly as she is. The one milking leaves the cow. The one boiling milk leaves the pot on the fire. The one cooking leaves the food unserved. The one feeding a child, the one waiting on her husband, the one eating her own dinner, all of them stand up and leave it. Some were in the middle of dressing or putting on makeup, and they go with their clothes and ornaments still in disarray. Their husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them, and they don't turn around. The Bhagavata adds that some were kept inside, unable to get out, and those women shut their eyes and went to him in meditation instead. Why linger on the half-finished jobs? Because the list is the point. Nobody in it has finished anything. Nobody waits for a better time, or tidies up, or makes herself presentable first. Devotional readers have heard in these lines a picture of the soul when God calls: it doesn't arrive polished, it arrives as it is, mid-task, with the milk still on the stove. And the Bhagavata doesn't let the scene pass unexamined. Right after this, the king who's listening stops the story to ask how a love like theirs could set anyone free, and Krishna himself will tell the women to go home. That is where we'll begin tomorrow. For tonight, the scene is enough. A village full of unfinished things, and a road into the trees with women on it, running toward a sound.
screen: `EACH ONE GOES EXACTLY AS SHE IS.` · `SOME KEPT INSIDE GO IN MEDITATION.` · `NOBODY FINISHES ANYTHING FIRST.` · then, large: `MID-TASK, AS SHE IS.`

segments.voice: Before you settle, notice what you've just set down to be here: a phone, a cup, a thought, a list. Don't tidy it. Leave it where it is. Now sit, and let your attention come here as you are, unfinished, not ready, no need to be. When the half-done things tug at you, notice the tug, and stay. If you pray, you can come to God, or to Krishna, just as you are in this moment, without fixing anything first. The bell holds the time.
The flute. On the autumn night, the sound that calls the gopis out of their houses, mid-task, just as they are.
Your line: mid-task, as she is. Today, when someone you love calls for you, try answering once before you finish what you're doing. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 899 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RASA LILA (WITH THE KEEPER'S FRAMING).`

900.title: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
900.hook: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
900.tomorrow: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
900.howItsDone: The rasa lila chapters of the Bhagavata are recited and sung by Krishna devotees and danced in the Ras Lila performances of Vrindavan and other places; teachers in the devotional traditions present them as a picture of the soul's love for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flute on the full-moon night: the gopis left the milk on the fire and the cow half milked, and went exactly as they were. When someone called for you, did you answer before you finished? Day nine hundred.

Before the dance, a king interrupts. In the Bhagavata, the sage Shuka is telling this story to King Parikshit, and Parikshit has just heard about the women running into the forest at night. He stops the story with a question. These women, he says, knew Krishna as a beloved, not as the highest truth. Their minds were full of him the way a lover's mind is full. How could that set them free? It's a fair question, and the text doesn't skip it. It answers before it goes one step further. Today, the rasa lila, and the frame the Bhagavata puts around it.
screen: `A KING INTERRUPTS.` → `THEY KNEW HIM AS A BELOVED.` → `HOW COULD THAT SET THEM FREE?`

segments.voice: Shuka's answer goes back to a story told earlier: Shishupala, a king who hated Krishna and spent his life thinking about him in rage, and still reached him in the end. If hatred fixed on him could do that, Shuka says, then whoever turns the whole mind toward him, whether in desire or anger, fear, affection, kinship or friendship, becomes absorbed in him. What matters is where the mind is pointed. That is the frame, and only then does the story go on. The women arrive, out of breath, and Krishna greets them like a polite host. Then he tells them to go home. The night is dark, he says, the forest is full of animals, your families will be looking for you, your place is with them. It's a test, and it lands hard. The gopis stand with their eyes down, scratching the ground with their toes, crying. Then they answer him. Their hearts, they say, were taken by him, and their feet won't carry them back. They didn't come for a household; they came for him. Krishna smiles, and stays, and the night of play in the forest begins. But it doesn't go smoothly for long. As he honors them, the women begin to feel proud, each one sure she is the most favored woman in the world. And at that moment, the text says, Krishna vanishes. Some devotional teachers read the whole episode as the soul's longing for God, told in the language of human love, and Parikshit's question is the text's own reminder to read it that way. Where he went, and whether they find him, is tomorrow.
screen: `WHERE THE MIND IS POINTED.` · `GO HOME, HE SAYS.` · `OUR FEET WON'T CARRY US BACK.` · then, large: `PRIDE, AND HE VANISHES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Shuka's answer was about where the mind is pointed. For these two minutes, notice where yours points on its own. Don't steer it. Just watch: a person, a worry, a hope, a plan. Each time you catch it, name the direction quietly, toward work, toward someone, toward tomorrow, and come back to the breath. If you pray, you can turn your mind toward God, or toward Krishna, for one breath, and then simply watch again. The bell holds the time.
Rasa lila. Krishna's night of dance and play with the gopis, which the Bhagavata frames as a story about where the whole mind is turned.
Your line: where the mind is pointed. Today, twice, stop and ask where your mind is pointed right now. Day nine hundred.

screen: `DAY 900 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RASA LILA (WITH THE KEEPER'S FRAMING).`

901.title: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
901.hook: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)
901.howItsDone: Devotees recite and sing the Gopi Gita from the Bhagavata, and the circle dance with Krishna between every two gopis is painted, sung, and performed in Ras Lila dance dramas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa lila began with a king's question and a frame: whoever turns the whole mind toward Krishna is absorbed in him. Then pride, and he vanished. Where was your mind pointed yesterday? Day nine hundred one.

Have you seen him? The gopis are asking the trees. They go from one to the next in the moonlit forest, a fig, a tulsi plant, a jasmine vine, asking each one whether he passed this way. Nobody answers. A moment ago they were sure they were the luckiest women alive, and now they are searching the forest floor for a footprint. Today, the second half of the rasa lila: the search, the song, and the circle.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN HIM?` → `ASKING THE TREES.` → `THE SEARCH, THE SONG, THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: They do find footprints, his, and beside them a woman's. He has taken one gopi with him. But she grows proud too, asks him to carry her, and he vanishes from her as well. The others find her weeping alone, and now they are all in the same place: together, without him. So they go down to the bank of the Yamuna and sing. Tradition calls their song the Gopi Gita. It has a reproach or two in it, but mostly it's a long remembering, his walk, his flute, his face coming home with the cows at dusk, and running through it, the plain plea to show himself. Then he's there, smiling, a garland around his neck. The gopis ask him a riddle about love: some love those who love them, some love those who don't, some love nobody. Which is he? Krishna answers that he stepped away so their love would deepen, the way a poor man who finds treasure and loses it thinks of nothing else. And then the one they worship says something startling: he can't repay them. Their own goodness, he tells them, will have to be their reward. Only then does the dance itself happen, the rasa. The women form a circle, and Krishna appears between every two of them, so that each one feels him at her side. The Bhagavata closes this story with one more frame for the listener: whoever hears it with faith, it says, gains devotion and is freed from the craving that troubles the heart. So a story this full of longing ends by calling itself medicine for craving.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS, AND A WOMAN'S BESIDE THEM.` · `THE SONG BY THE YAMUNA.` · `HE CAN'T REPAY THEM.` · then, large: `BETWEEN EVERY TWO, IN THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath come and go. The gopis found him again by remembering, not by searching harder. For these two minutes, try remembering. Bring back one moment when you felt close to someone, or to something larger than yourself. Don't chase the feeling. Recall the details: where you were, the light, a sound. Stay with the details, and let whatever comes come. If you pray, you can remember a moment of nearness to God, or to Krishna, in the same way. The bell holds the time.
Rasa lila. The night of the circle dance, where Krishna appears between every two gopis, after they search for him and sing.
Your line: between every two. Today, when you miss someone, spend one minute remembering a detail instead of the absence. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: leaving Vrindavan
902.howItsDone: Akrura is remembered by devotees as a model of longing to see God; the chapters of his journey to Vraja are recited from the Bhagavata, and pilgrims to the Vrindavan area visit places linked with the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa lila ended: the search, the song by the river, and the circle with Krishna between every two gopis. What did you remember, when you missed someone yesterday? Day nine hundred two.

A chariot is on the road to Vraja, and the man driving it is carrying a trap. King Kamsa of Mathura has learned that the cowherd boy everyone talks about is the son he was warned of, the one born to kill him. So Kamsa plans a festival, a contest of wrestlers, and an elephant at the gate. All he needs is someone the boys will trust to bring them. He chooses Akrura, a respected elder of their own clan. Akrura agrees to go. Today the story turns toward the road out of the village: leaving Vrindavan.
screen: `A CHARIOT CARRYING A TRAP.` → `KAMSA NEEDS A MESSENGER.` → `AKRURA AGREES TO GO.`

segments.voice: Here is the surprise. Akrura is Kamsa's messenger, and Krishna's devotee. The Bhagavata spends the whole ride inside his head, and what's in there isn't dread. It's longing. All the way down the road he is turning one thought over: I'm going to see him. He wonders whether Krishna will look at him kindly, whether he'll be welcomed or held at arm's length as the king's man. He counts the long errand as good fortune, because of where it ends. He reaches Vraja at sunset, when the cows are coming home. And in the dust of the cow pen he sees footprints, and he knows whose they are; the text says they carry the marks devotees look for on the soles of Krishna's feet. Akrura jumps down from his chariot and rolls in that dust, overcome. Then Krishna and Balarama come out to meet him. They don't hold him at arm's length. The brothers embrace him, take his hand, lead him in, wash his feet and feed him. Krishna asks after his family, and only then asks what brought him. And Akrura, the king's messenger, tells them everything: Kamsa's hatred, the festival, the plan. Krishna and Balarama laugh, and agree to go. So the road out of Vrindavan begins with a man who came carrying the king's summons, and spent the journey hoping. Two loyalties ride in that chariot, and the story doesn't scold him for either one. It just lets us watch a man doing a hard errand with his heart pointed somewhere else.
screen: `THE KING'S MAN, AND KRISHNA'S DEVOTEE.` · `FOOTPRINTS IN THE DUST.` · `WASHED, FED, ASKED AFTER.` · then, large: `HE TELLS THEM EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind one errand or duty ahead of you that you'd rather not do. Hold it lightly. Now look past it, the way Akrura looked down the road: who or what will be at the end of it? A person, a finished job, a quiet evening. Breathe with that. You don't have to love the errand. Just let your heart point at what it's for. If you pray, you can offer the errand to God, or to Krishna, before you begin it. The bell holds the time.
Leaving Vrindavan. The turn in the Bhagavata when Akrura comes from Mathura with Kamsa's summons, and Krishna agrees to go.
Your line: Akrura in the dust. Today, before a task you dread, name one good thing waiting at the far end of it. Day nine hundred two.

903.title: leaving Vrindavan
903.howItsDone: The gopis' grief at Krishna's departure is a theme of devotional poetry and song, and devotees in the Vrindavan area remember the place associated with his leaving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, leaving Vrindavan began on the road: Akrura, the king's messenger, riding toward Vraja full of longing, rolling in the dust of Krishna's footprints. What waited at the end of your hard errand? Day nine hundred three.

The news gets around the village overnight. By morning everyone knows: Akrura has come from Mathura, and he is taking Krishna and Balarama with him. The cowherd men are loading carts with pots of milk and butter as gifts for the king. And the gopis, who ran into the forest at the sound of a flute, are standing in the road beside the chariot. This time there's nothing to run toward. Today, leaving Vrindavan, from the side of the ones who stay.
screen: `THE NEWS GETS AROUND OVERNIGHT.` → `CARTS LOADED FOR MATHURA.` → `THE ONES WHO STAY.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the gopis a long, raw lament, and it doesn't tidy it up. They blame the creator, who brings people together and then pulls them apart for no reason, like a child playing and spoiling the game. They turn on Akrura too. His name means not cruel, they say, and it doesn't fit him: he's come to carry off the one thing they have. They talk about the women of Mathura, who will see Krishna every day now, and wonder whether a city boy will remember village girls. Then they stop worrying about what anyone thinks, and they cry out his names in the road. The chariot starts to move. Krishna sees them, and he sends back word through a messenger, as the text puts it: I will come back. And the gopis stand where they are, watching, until the flag on the chariot and the dust behind it are gone. That ends this week, and look at its shape. It began with a flute that stopped the cows in the pasture. Then the gopi jealous of a hollow reed. Then a full-moon night with the milk left on the fire, and the frame: where the whole mind is turned. Then the search, the song, and a circle with Krishna beside every one. And now the same women in the road, with the same longing, and nowhere to go. The Bhagavata doesn't treat the parting as the end of their love. Some devotional teachers say it's where that love is tested most deeply, in remembering him from a distance. The story will come back to these women. For now, a promise, a cloud of dust, and the road.
screen: `THEY BLAME THE CREATOR, AND AKRURA.` · `I WILL COME BACK.` · `UNTIL THE DUST IS GONE.` · then, large: `A WEEK OF LONGING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has left, for a trip, a new city, a new life, or further. Let yourself be the one standing in the road. Notice the ache if it's there, and don't push it away. Then, gently, recall one thing they gave you that stayed: a habit, a phrase, a way of laughing. Breathe with that. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, or before Krishna, without asking for anything. The bell holds the time.
Leaving Vrindavan. The morning Krishna's chariot leaves for Mathura, and the gopis watch until the flag and the dust are gone.
Your line: until the dust is gone. Today, send one short message to someone far away: a promise small enough to keep. Day nine hundred three.
